config.title: Network Awareness & Resilience

intro.title: Network Awareness & Resilience
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a mobile app that detects when the device is online or offline and displays a clear status message to the user. You will learn the core concept of network awareness by using the Capacitor Network API to listen for connectivity changes. The main technologies involved are Ionic for the UI, Angular for the app structure, and Capacitor for native device access. By the end, you'll have a resilient app that can gracefully handle network interruptions.
intro.usecase: Network awareness is crucial in mobile apps where connectivity can be unreliable. In ride-sharing apps like Uber, the UI shows 'offline mode' indicators and cached trip history when network drops. E-commerce apps like Amazon display cached product listings and queue cart updates until reconnection. Travel apps like Airbnb show saved itineraries and sync booking attempts automatically when back online. Implementing these patterns prevents user frustration and data loss during connectivity changes.

objectives: Import and inject the Ionic Network service into an Angular component to access network status functionality.
Define a network status state variable using TypeScript interfaces to store current connection information.
Implement a subscription handler to monitor network status changes in real-time.
Execute conditional logic to display different UI elements based on online/offline connection state.
Apply Angular lifecycle hooks (ngOnInit, ngOnDestroy) to properly initialize and clean up network subscriptions.
Construct a user interface with Ionic components that visually indicates the current network status.
Utilize the Capacitor Network plugin to retrieve the initial network connection state on app startup.
Handle network disconnection events by storing pending data operations in local storage for later synchronization.
Modify application behavior to queue API requests when offline and retry them when connectivity is restored.
Implement a retry mechanism with exponential backoff to handle transient network failures during API calls.
Use Ionic loading controllers to provide user feedback during network state transitions and retry operations.
Apply network-aware routing guards to prevent navigation to data-intensive pages when offline.

steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the component names from '@ionic/angular' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Import Capacitor Network plugin
steps.instruction: Import the Network plugin from '@capacitor/network' to enable network status detection.
steps.hint: Use a standard ES6 import statement to bring in the Network module from the specified package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing a Capacitor plugin
import { Network } from '@capacitor/network';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Network plugin is imported and available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The import statement for Network from '@capacitor/network' is correctly added.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Capacitor Network plugin. This gives you access to network status APIs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check the import syntax. Make sure you're importing from '@capacitor/network'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import Network from '@capacitor/network'.

steps.title: Create the NetworkStatus component
steps.instruction: Create a standalone Angular component named NetworkStatus with the @Component decorator, setting standalone: true and selector: 'app-network-status'.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator from '@angular/core' to define your component class.
steps.expectedOutcome: A standalone Angular component class named NetworkStatus is created with the correct decorator configuration.
successCriteria:
The component must:
1. Have the @Component decorator
2. Set standalone: true
3. Have selector: 'app-network-status'
4. Be exported as a class named NetworkStatus
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully created the NetworkStatus component with the correct standalone configuration. This component will serve as the foundation for displaying network status information.
steps.feedbackPartial:

1. Used the @Component decorator
2. Set standalone: true
3. Used selector: 'app-network-status'
4. Exported the class as NetworkStatus
Check your syntax and try again.

steps.title: Define component template imports
steps.instruction: Add the imports array to the @Component decorator, including CommonModule and the Ionic UI components imported earlier.
steps.hint: The imports array should be placed inside the @Component decorator and list the modules/components needed for the template.
steps.expectedOutcome: The @Component decorator now has an imports array containing CommonModule and the Ionic components.
successCriteria: The component decorator includes an imports array with at least CommonModule, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, and IonContent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've properly added the imports array to the component decorator. This makes the CommonModule and Ionic components available for use in your template.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an imports array, but it might be missing some required modules. Make sure to include CommonModule and all four Ionic components (IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent).
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports array is missing or incorrect. Remember to add the imports array inside the @Component decorator with the required modules.

steps.title: Initialize network status state
steps.instruction: Inside the NetworkStatus component class, define a TypeScript interface named NetworkStatus with two properties: 'connected' (boolean) and 'connectionType' (string).
steps.hint: Define the interface first, then add the property to your component class. Use TypeScript syntax for both the interface and property declaration.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a typed networkStatus property with default values, ready to store actual network information.
successCriteria: The code should include: 1) A NetworkStatus interface with correct properties, 2) A networkStatus property of that type, 3) Default initialization values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the NetworkStatus interface and initialized the networkStatus property with default values. This gives us a typed structure to store network connectivity information.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but something is missing. Make sure you've defined both the NetworkStatus interface (with connected: boolean and connectionType: string) AND the networkStatus property initialized with default values (connected: false, connectionType: 'unknown').
steps.feedbackWrong: The code doesn't match what was requested. You need to define a NetworkStatus interface with two properties (connected: boolean, connectionType: string) and then create a networkStatus property of that type with default values inside the component class.

steps.title: Initialize network listener state
steps.instruction: Inside the NetworkStatusComponent class, create a property named networkListener with type any to store the network status change listener.
steps.hint: Add a class property declaration with the type annotation ': any'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class now has a networkListener property ready to store the network status listener.
successCriteria: The NetworkStatusComponent class contains a property declaration for networkListener with type any.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the networkListener property. This will be used to store the network status change listener so we can properly manage and clean it up later.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the networkListener property isn't quite complete. Make sure you've declared it with the correct name and type annotation ': any'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The networkListener property is missing or incorrect. You need to add a property declaration inside the NetworkStatusComponent class with the name 'networkListener' and type 'any'.

steps.title: Create method to get initial network status
steps.instruction: Inside the NetworkStatusComponent class, create an async method named getNetworkStatus that calls Network.getStatus() and updates the networkStatus property with the result.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before the method name. Call Network.getStatus() which returns a Promise. Use await to get the result and assign it to this.networkStatus.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has an async method that can fetch the current network status from the Capacitor Network plugin.
successCriteria: The method must be named getNetworkStatus, be marked as async, call Network.getStatus(), and assign the result to this.networkStatus.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the getNetworkStatus method that will fetch the initial network status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Is the method async? Does it call Network.getStatus()? Does it assign the result to this.networkStatus?
steps.feedbackWrong: The method isn't quite right. Remember to create an async method named getNetworkStatus that calls Network.getStatus() and updates the networkStatus property.

steps.title: Create method to start network monitoring
steps.instruction: Inside the NetworkStatusComponent class, create a method named startNetworkListener that will set up a listener for network status changes using the Network plugin.
steps.hint: Define a method that calls Network.addListener() and stores the returned listener in the networkListener property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a startNetworkListener method defined that will be ready to monitor network changes.
successCriteria: The method should be named startNetworkListener, be defined inside the NetworkStatusComponent class, and include a call to Network.addListener.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the startNetworkListener method. This method will be responsible for monitoring network status changes when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the method is named exactly 'startNetworkListener' and includes the Network.addListener call. Check your syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The startNetworkListener method is not properly defined. Ensure you create a method with the correct name inside the NetworkStatusComponent class.

steps.title: Implement Angular lifecycle methods
steps.instruction: Inside the NetworkStatusComponent class, implement the ngOnInit lifecycle method. In this method, call both the getNetworkStatus() and startNetworkListener() methods.
steps.hint: Use the ngOnInit() method from Angular's lifecycle hooks. Call the existing methods inside it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now automatically initialize network status and start monitoring when it loads.
successCriteria: The component class should have an ngOnInit method that calls getNetworkStatus() and startNetworkListener().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've implemented the ngOnInit lifecycle method to initialize network monitoring when the component loads.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure ngOnInit calls both getNetworkStatus() and startNetworkListener().
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnInit method should be implemented in the component class and call both existing methods.

steps.title: Clean up network listener on destroy
steps.instruction: Implement the ngOnDestroy lifecycle method in your component to properly clean up the network listener when the component is destroyed.
steps.hint: Angular's ngOnDestroy method is called just before the component is destroyed. Inside this method, check if the networkListener property exists and remove it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now properly clean up the network listener when it's destroyed, preventing memory leaks.
successCriteria: The ngOnDestroy method should be implemented, check if networkListener exists, and call remove() on it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented ngOnDestroy to clean up the network listener. This prevents memory leaks by removing the listener when the component is destroyed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check if networkListener exists before trying to remove it, and call the remove() method on it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnDestroy method should be implemented to clean up the network listener. Check if networkListener exists and call remove() on it.

steps.title: Create the component template structure
steps.instruction: Create the component's template with basic Ionic UI structure: an IonHeader containing IonToolbar and IonTitle, and an IonContent wrapper.
steps.hint: Add a template property to the @Component decorator with the Ionic UI structure. Use the Ionic components you imported earlier.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a basic Ionic component template structure
@Component({
  selector: 'app-example',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule, IonContent, IonHeader, IonTitle, IonToolbar],
  template: `
    <ion-header>
      <ion-toolbar>
        <ion-title>Example Title</ion-title>
      </ion-toolbar>
    </ion-header>
    <ion-content>
      <!-- Content will go here -->
    </ion-content>
  `
})
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a basic Ionic UI structure with header and content areas ready for network status display.
successCriteria: The @Component decorator should include a template property with the required Ionic structure containing ion-header, ion-toolbar, ion-title, and ion-content elements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the basic Ionic UI structure for your component. The template now has the header and content areas ready for displaying network information.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a template, but it's missing some required Ionic elements. Make sure your template includes: ion-header with ion-toolbar and ion-title inside, and an ion-content wrapper.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component template structure is not properly implemented. You need to add a template property to the @Component decorator with the Ionic UI structure using the imported Ionic components.

steps.title: Display network status in template
steps.instruction: Add an IonCard to your component's template that displays the network connection status using an IonBadge (with color based on connected state) and shows the connection type.
steps.hint: Use *ngIf to conditionally apply CSS classes to IonBadge based on networkStatus.connected, and display networkStatus.connectionType in the IonCard content.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of conditional styling and data binding in Ionic Angular template Network Status {{ isConnected ? 'Online' : 'Offline' }}

Connection type: {{ connectionType }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The template now displays network status information with visual feedback using Ionic components.
successCriteria: IonBadge component present with conditional styling
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully bound the network status data to the template with conditional visual feedback. The IonBadge now clearly shows whether the device is online or offline, and the connection type is displayed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some of the required elements. Make sure you have: 1) An IonCard component, 2) An IonBadge that changes appearance based on networkStatus.connected, 3) The connection type displayed from networkStatus.connectionType.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't yet display the network status information. You need to add an IonCard containing an IonBadge that shows connection status (with color based on connected state) and displays the connection type.
